#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Read-only worktree prune audit. Classifies every git worktree by size, merge
# state, uncommitted work, remote/PR state, and the most recent chat that
# operated in it. Emits a table sorted by size with a suggested bucket. Never
# deletes anything; deletion stays a human-gated step in the playbook.
#
# Usage: worktree-audit.sh [-b|--base <ref>] [repo-path]
#   repo-path defaults to the current repo.
#   -b sets the ref the MERGED column checks against (e.g. origin/integration).
#   Without it the base is origin/HEAD, then origin/main, then origin/master.
#   origin/HEAD is the remote's default branch, not necessarily the branch PRs
#   merge into; pass -b when they differ.
set -u

base=""
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
	case "$1" in
	-b|--base) [ $# -ge 2 ] || { echo "error: $1 needs a ref" >&2; exit 2; }; base="$2"; shift 2 ;;
	-h|--help) sed -n '2,/^set -u/p' "$0" | sed '$d; s/^# \{0,1\}//'; exit 0 ;;
	-*) echo "error: unknown option: $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
	*) break ;;
	esac
done

repo="${1:-$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null)}"
[ -z "$repo" ] && { echo "not in a git repo; pass a repo path" >&2; exit 1; }
cd "$repo" || exit 1
git rev-parse --git-dir >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "error: not a git repo: $repo" >&2; exit 1; }

# Main worktree is the first entry; everything else is a candidate.
main_wt=$(git worktree list --porcelain | awk '/^worktree /{print $2; exit}')

if [ -z "$base" ]; then
	for cand in "$(git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD 2>/dev/null)" origin/main origin/master; do
		[ -n "$cand" ] && git rev-parse --verify --quiet "$cand^{commit}" >/dev/null && { base="$cand"; break; }
	done
	[ -z "$base" ] && { echo "error: no base ref (origin/HEAD, origin/main, origin/master all missing); pass -b <ref>" >&2; exit 1; }
	echo "warn: no -b given; MERGED checks against $base" >&2
fi

# The base drives the merge check. The fetch is best-effort (stale is fine for
# a first pass) and runs before the check, since -b may name a branch not
# fetched yet. The explicit refspec creates it even in a single-branch clone.
case "$base" in
origin/*) git fetch origin "+refs/heads/${base#origin/}:refs/remotes/$base" --quiet 2>/dev/null \
	|| echo "warn: could not fetch $base; merged column may be stale" >&2 ;;
esac
git rev-parse --verify --quiet "$base^{commit}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "error: base ref not found: $base" >&2; exit 1; }

# GNU coreutils (Linux, Homebrew gnubin) reads `stat -f` as file system status
# and `date -r` as a file, so pick the stat and date flags once.
if stat -c %Y / >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	stat_fmt=(-c '%Y %n'); fmt_day() { date -d "@$1" '+%Y-%m-%d'; }
else
	stat_fmt=(-f '%m %N'); fmt_day() { date -r "$1" '+%Y-%m-%d'; }
fi

# PR state by branch, fetched once as [{number, state, head}] with a lowercase
# state. Origin when its CLI can read this repo's PRs, otherwise gh. Empty when
# neither can.
prs=$(mktemp)
if command -v origin >/dev/null 2>&1 \
	&& raw=$(origin pr list --author "@me" --state all --limit 1000 \
		--json number,status,headRef 2>/dev/null); then
	printf '%s' "$raw" | jq '[.[] | {number, state: .status, head: .headRef}]' > "$prs" 2>/dev/null
elif raw=$(gh pr list --author "@me" --state all --limit 1000 \
	--json number,state,headRefName 2>/dev/null); then
	printf '%s' "$raw" | jq '[.[] | {number, state: (.state | ascii_downcase), head: .headRefName}]' > "$prs" 2>/dev/null
fi
[ -s "$prs" ] || echo "[]" > "$prs"

# Transcripts dir: ~/.cursor/projects/<slugified-repo-path>/agent-transcripts.
slug=$(printf '%s' "$main_wt" | sed 's#^/##; s#/#-#g')
transcripts="$HOME/.cursor/projects/$slug/agent-transcripts"
now=$(date +%s)

echo "# base: $base"
printf "SIZE\tAGE\tMERGED\tDIRTY\tREMOTE\tPR\tLAST_CHAT\tBUCKET\tWORKTREE\n"

git worktree list --porcelain | awk '/^worktree /{print $2}' | while read -r wt; do
	[ "$wt" = "$main_wt" ] && continue

	size=$(du -sh "$wt" 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1}')
	head=$(git -C "$wt" rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null)
	head_ts=$(git -C "$wt" log -1 --format='%ct' HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
	age=$([ "$head_ts" -gt 0 ] 2>/dev/null && echo "$(( (now - head_ts) / 86400 ))d" || echo "?")

	# Squash-merged branches are not ancestors of the base, so PR state is the
	# real signal; merge-base only catches fast-forward/rebase merges.
	git merge-base --is-ancestor "$head" "$base" 2>/dev/null && merged=YES || merged=no

	# Distinguish real WIP (tracked edits) from disposable untracked scratch.
	porcelain=$(git -C "$wt" status --porcelain 2>/dev/null)
	if [ -z "$porcelain" ]; then dirty=clean
	elif printf '%s\n' "$porcelain" | grep -qv '^??'; then
		dirty="wip:$(printf '%s\n' "$porcelain" | grep -cv '^??')"
	else dirty="scratch:$(printf '%s\n' "$porcelain" | grep -c '^??')"; fi

	branch=$(git -C "$wt" symbolic-ref --quiet --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo "")
	if [ -z "$branch" ]; then remote=detached
	elif git -C "$wt" show-ref --verify --quiet "refs/remotes/origin/$branch"; then
		[ "$(git -C "$wt" rev-parse "origin/$branch" 2>/dev/null)" = "$head" ] \
			&& remote=pushed \
			|| remote="ahead$(git -C "$wt" rev-list --count "origin/$branch..HEAD" 2>/dev/null)"
	else remote=no-remote; fi

	pr=$([ -n "$branch" ] && jq -r --arg b "$branch" \
		'.[] | select(.head==$b) | "#\(.number)/\(.state)"' "$prs" 2>/dev/null | head -1)
	[ -z "$pr" ] && pr="-"

	# Most recent chat whose transcript operated in this worktree. Match path
	# followed by "/" or a quote so glint-482 does not match glint-482-r37.
	last="-"; last_ts=0
	if [ -d "$transcripts" ]; then
		f=$(rg -l -e "${wt}/" -e "${wt}\"" "$transcripts" 2>/dev/null \
			| xargs stat "${stat_fmt[@]}" 2>/dev/null | sort -rn | head -1)
		if [ -n "$f" ]; then last_ts=$(echo "$f" | awk '{print $1}')
			last=$(fmt_day "$last_ts" 2>/dev/null); fi
	fi
	recent=$([ "$last_ts" -gt 0 ] 2>/dev/null && [ $(( (now - last_ts) / 86400 )) -le 4 ] && echo yes || echo no)

	case "$dirty" in wip:*) bucket=hold-wip ;; *)
		case "$pr" in */open|*/draft) bucket=hold-open-pr ;; *)
			if [ "$recent" = yes ]; then bucket=verify-recent-chat
			elif [ "$merged" = YES ] || [ "$pr" != "-" ]; then bucket=safe
			else bucket=review; fi ;;
		esac ;;
	esac

	printf "%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n" \
		"$size" "$age" "$merged" "$dirty" "$remote" "$pr" "$last" "$bucket" "$wt"
done | sort -t$'\t' -k1,1 -rh

rm -f "$prs"

### Autonomous run

**You own the exit condition. Define done, then drive to it without stopping.**

1. State the exit condition as a checkable predicate before the first iteration (tests green, repro fixed, all N PRs merged, pixel-diff zero).
2. Pick the wake mechanism using Cursor's `/loop` command (a built-in, not a pstack skill). An event to watch (CI, a merge, a ref advancing) gets a watcher subagent that wakes you on the event, with a long time-based heartbeat as fallback. No event gets a fixed-interval heartbeat sized to when the result is worth re-checking. Pick each subagent's reasoning level for the job, per the Subagents section.
3. Each iteration makes the smallest change the evidence justifies, verifies it against the predicate, commits if it advanced, discards changes that didn't help. Belt-and-suspenders that "might help" gets reverted, not left to ride.
   Sequence the work via the **sequence-verifiable-units** principle skill, verifying each unit before the next instead of batching checks at the end.
4. Mid-run discoveries that support the goal are yours. Address broken skills, related bugs, flaky verifiers, review noise, tooling failures, orphaned follow-ups, and fixable drift yourself via poteto-mode. Put out-of-band fixes in their own PR. Do not park reversible work for the human or use `AskQuestion`. Surface only irreversible actions, genuine product or preference calls no experiment can settle, or a real dead end. Keep the predicate as the main drive, and return to it after each side fix.
5. Checkpoint every iteration via the **show-me-your-work** skill, a row for what changed and whether the predicate moved.
6. Stop when the predicate is met. A plateau is not a stop, so keep going and pivot your approach to push past it. Surface a genuine dead end rather than spinning, and never relax the predicate to declare victory.

### Autopilot-full

**You own the verdicts, never the PRs. One owner carries each PR from build to merge, and nothing merges until your swarm, which never wrote the code, has proven the code that lands.**

A verdict covers one patch and green CI covers one head. Step 4 runs a full swarm once, and again only for a major change. The patch-id rule in `playbooks/shipping.md` can carry a lane's result, and every new head needs its own green CI.

1. **The operator's gates come first.** The grant covers only the queue's items, so items the operator names as theirs and PRs outside the queue stop at merge-ready. A request to state the plan is not a go.
2. **Spawn one owner per PR, and keep its work where a replacement can find it.** Resolve the forge once for the program. GitHub CLI (`gh`) is the default. If `command -v origin` succeeds and Origin can resolve the repository, use `origin pr` for every PR operation. Otherwise stay on `gh` and record the fallback. Never require Graphite (`gt`). Each owner is a Cursor cloud agent that builds, opens its PR per `playbooks/opening-a-pr.md`, proves the change on the real artifact, babysits to green per `playbooks/babysit.md`, and merges once steps 4 and 5 clear it. Where that playbook says to report a rebase, the owner rebases its own branch and publishes it with `git push --force-with-lease`.

   Open the PR early so CI and bots run alongside the work. The code is ready only after the slop-strip (the `deslop` skill from the `cursor-team-kit` plugin (`/deslop`)) and the `/no-comments` pass, so the full swarm runs on finished code. Then rebase onto current trunk and report the code-ready head before self-proof, so verification runs on the base the patch lands on. Report every later head, and merge-ready once self-proof, CI, and babysit are done. Fix rounds stay on that base unless trunk conflicts, breaks CI, or lands a known concurrent change to the same files, because each rebase restarts CI. Run the repo's checks for the touched paths on the committed head before the code-ready push and before a later push that needs a verifier.

   Assume the VM dies. Soon after starting, push and start a decision trail in the root agent's store (path in the system prompt) per the **show-me-your-work** skill, then push each finished unit before you start the next. Whoever spawns a subagent records its id, state, and a stuck-after runtime from past runs of its kind in that store, so the root can probe it if the parent dies. Force-push only your own branch, with `--force-with-lease` pinned to the SHA you last pushed or took over, and on any push you did not make, stop and report to the root.
3. **Run owners in parallel off trunk, never stacked,** so each PR lands on its own.
4. **Swarm-verify once.** A full swarm runs once, at the code-ready head. Another full swarm runs only for new behavior, a redesign, or a large new diff. A rebase, a merge-conflict resolution, or a minor fix gets a single verifier at the new head, and a wording-only change gets none. Fan out independent verifiers at the code-ready SHA per the **swarm** skill. They re-run the gates, prove the load-bearing behavior live on the real surface through its control skill (such as `control-ui` or `control-cli` from `cursor-team-kit`) or a named driver, and audit the diff. The verdict is not clean without the live lane, or before you audit the merge-ready report's receipts, because no lane trusts a claim it has not checked.

   Block a PR only for a problem you can show, with a failing run at the head or a doc line the PR made wrong. A problem the PR's base already has, whether trunk or the PR below it in a stack, doesn't block unless the PR copies it or newly reaches it. Only a bug a user would hit, a failed gate, or a wrong shipped doc blocks, and everything else goes in a follow-up.
5. **The owner merges only what you verified, tested on the trunk it lands on.** Green CI alone never authorizes a merge. Once the swarm's lanes have started, merge prep rebases onto current trunk, reports the new head, and waits for green CI.

   Right before merging, fetch trunk and ask whether its changes can affect the patch, because rebasing for every trunk move never ends. Rebase and wait for CI when the code that would land was never tested, as with a conflict, a file both sides changed, or a change to which checks run for the PR. A lockfile both sides changed needs no rebase when a frozen install passes on the merge result and the packages the PR changes resolve there as on the head, because that install tests the lockfile that would land, and a failing install means the rebase must repair it. When trunk changed a caller of the patch or something the patch depends on, such as code it calls or a dependency version, run the patch's checks on the merge result and merge on a pass. Otherwise merge. If trunk would force a third rebase past merge prep, hold and report to the root, which sequences the colliding work.
6. **Run the root layer.** Anything that loosens a gate, such as a raised budget or an allowlist entry, needs a verifier's proof and then your fresh countersign, because the owner is the one who wants green. Under a grant that covers approvals, that countersign is the approval, and the owner's record of it points at your countersign for a lane to check. A disabled or soft-failed check always comes out, because it stops guarding every case. Never give or bypass an approval the forge enforces, because no countersign covers it.

   On the operator's go, arm `/loop 1h` to audit until no delegated work is left, because long runs drift and agents stall silently. Each tick re-reads this playbook from trunk and fixes drift, such as an unreported head or an unrecorded agent, by having its owner record it, because drift is a gap in the record, not a stall. It probes every agent, down to the leaf lanes, and judges each by its side effects, because status text and summaries can hide a stuck child. An agent is stuck when it errors, cannot start turns, or shows nothing new past its stuck-after runtime, and so is an owner that has neither pushed nor written a trail row by the first tick. One waiting on you or the operator is not stuck, so answer it. Replace a stuck agent at once, without waiting for its stop to land. A tick that changed something for the operator ends by catching them up per the **ketchup** skill, and one that changed nothing stays quiet.
7. **Stand down at once on the operator's stop.** A hold reaches every owner as a zero-writes order. Each reports where it stands and keeps its brief until the operator releases it.

**Reply:** catch the operator up per the **ketchup** skill, covering each PR's state and verdict, what merged, countersigns and why, open operator gates, and parked follow-ups, with links to each PR and the trails.

### Hillclimb

**You own the metric and the experiment's integrity. Supervise and review. Delegate the attempts.** For sustained, iterative improvement of one measurable thing against a target. A one-off fix is Bug fix or Perf issue. This is the loop.

1. Ground the workload and architecture before choosing the metric. Trace the target, name the realistic workload dimensions that can move the result (data size, history, state, concurrency), and select a case that reproduces the user's complaint. If no case reproduces it, fix the repro instead of hillclimbing. Then fix one metric, the direction that counts as better, and a checkable stop predicate that pairs a target with a floor on attempts so a lucky early win can't end the run (the example "at least 50% better than baseline and at least 10 iterations" is this shape). Use the user's numbers when given, otherwise agree them.
2. Build the measurement harness, prove its sensitivity, then freeze it (the **build-the-lever** principle skill). Run contrasting realistic workloads and confirm the target case reproduces the symptom while easier cases separate as expected. If the harness cannot distinguish them, revise the workload or metric. Vet the harness with the **benchmark-checklist** skill before you freeze it, and make it print its error count and a count of the work done. Once frozen, one repeatable command emits the metric, sampled enough to clear the noise (median of N, not a single run). Record the baseline metric and a green run of the regression gate (the tests that must keep passing) before any change.
3. Open the decision log via the **show-me-your-work** skill. A `decision.tsv`, one row per attempt: id, hypothesis, change, before, after, delta, tests, verdict (kept or reverted), note. Read it before each attempt. Keep it out of the tree (gitignored).

   - Hand the change to a subagent using your configured hillclimb model (default `claude-opus-5-5-xhigh-fast`) with a tight scope. ### Refactoring

**You own the contract. The structure changes. The behavior does not.** Distinct from Feature, which adds behavior, and Bug fix, which corrects it.

If the cleanup reveals a missing feature or a real bug, split it out and ship the structural change first against the pinned contract. A redesign is allowed, but name it and route to Feature. Large or cross-cutting structural work belongs to the **figure-it-out** skill. This playbook is the focused-to-medium change.

1. Pin the behavior contract first. Trace the affected subsystem to learn the contract, then write a characterization test, snapshot, or equivalence harness that captures current behavior before any structure moves. If the area has no coverage, write the pin before touching structure. Type check and lint are not a pin.
2. Name the structure the code is missing per **principle-model-the-domain**. Boring code stays when the shape is already clear and local. The reshape must delete branches or invalid states, not add indirection.
3. Name the target shape. State what the module layout, types, and call graph should be if built today (**principle-foundational-thinking**, **principle-redesign-from-first-principles**). If the target crosses a function boundary, run the **architect** skill for the shape before the move.
4. Subtract before you add. Delete dead code, collapse one-caller wrappers, drop redundant validators, and remove orphan references before introducing the new shape (**principle-subtract-before-you-add**). The smallest change that reaches the target shape ships (**principle-laziness-protocol**). A speculative cleanup that "might help" gets reverted.
5. Move in small behavior-preserving steps, each keeping the pin green. For API reshapes, migrate every caller and delete the old API in the same wave (**principle-migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis**). No compatibility shims, no parallel old-and-new paths. Spot-check every rename against the actual files. Renames silently miss usages in strings, prose, and back-references. Delegate the mechanical edits to a subagent using your configured refactoring model (default `claude-opus-5-5-xhigh-fast`) with a specific scope (file paths, the names being moved, the behavior to hold). Pick each subagent's reasoning level for the job, per the Subagents section.
6. Prove behavior is unchanged on the real artifact, not "it compiles" (**principle-prove-it-works**). For larger reshapes, run an equivalence check: a script that diffs old-vs-new outputs, a recorded baseline replayed against the new code, or a smoke run on the matching surface via the relevant control skill.
7. Confirm the change is worth keeping. The success measure is reduced reader load (**principle-minimize-reader-load**). If the diff does not lower reader load somewhere, revert it.

### Shipping

**You own what lands. Verify each PR independently, land only the verified run from the root, then keep your hands off the stack.**

1. **Resolve the forge, then verify each PR independently before it lands.** GitHub CLI (`gh`) is the default. If `command -v origin` succeeds and Origin can resolve the repository, use `origin pr` for every PR operation. Otherwise stay on `gh` and record the fallback. Never require Graphite (`gt`). One verifier per PR, each a Cursor cloud agent, runs the change the way a user would with the matching control skill (such as `control-ui` or `control-cli` from `cursor-team-kit`), parent against head, and posts `PASS`, `PASS+NOTES`, or `FAIL` on that PR. Only a verdict from an agent that did not write the code counts, because an author checks what it meant to build. Green CI and an approving bot review are not verdicts, because neither runs the change as a user would.
2. **Land only the contiguous verified run rooted at the bottom.** Walk up from the lowest unmerged PR and stop at the first one without `PASS` or `PASS+NOTES`. The PRs below it are the run, and the top one is the ceiling. A verified PR above an unverified one waits, because it cannot land without the code below it. One whose branch neither holds nor needs that code can move onto trunk and land on its own. It needs a fresh verdict first, because its old one ran with that code beneath it and trunk does not have it.
3. **Re-check that the verdicts still describe the code.** A verdict covers a patch, and a chain rebase moves every PR above it to a new SHA without failing any check. Compare `git patch-id` at the verdict SHA with the current head before trusting an older verdict. When the patches differ only in tests, docs, or lint config, a lane's result stands if what it ran builds the same at both SHAs apart from noise. Noise is a difference that also shows up between two builds of the verdict SHA, or an embedded commit SHA. Report each kind of noise with its files, so a reader can check the call. The change itself still gets fresh checks and a review, because the old verdict never saw it. A lane with no build output, such as a dev server, cannot show this, so rerun it, and re-verify anything else that drifted.
4. **Land bottom-up, one PR at a time.** Always merge the run's lowest unmerged PR, with `origin pr merge <pr>` or `gh pr merge <pr> --squash`. On Origin the plain command also merges every PR below the one you name, and on GitHub a PR whose base is still its parent's branch merges into that branch, not trunk. Read the PR back for the result (`origin pr view <pr>` or `gh pr view <pr> --json state,mergedAt,baseRefName`), because a merge command can report success when a merge queue only queued the PR, and a requested auto-merge is not a merge. A landed PR reads merged with trunk as its base, not its parent's branch. Arm `--auto` (Origin merge-when-ready or GitHub auto-merge) only on a PR whose verdict covers its current head, because it lands whatever head is ready. After a merge lands, retarget the PR whose base was the merged branch to trunk (`origin pr edit <pr> --base <trunk>` or `gh pr edit <pr> --base <trunk>`), move its patch onto the merge result, and push with `--force-with-lease`. The verdict covers the patch, not its commits, so step 3's patch-id rule decides whether the verdict survives. Merge it once its checks pass and its verdict survives.
5. **Leave the stack alone while it lands.** Step 4's move of the next PR is the only change to a branch or base, because a merge lands whatever its branch and base hold at that moment, verdict or not. On GitHub, watch the run with `scripts/watch-pr/watch-pr --queued-stack` under `/loop` until it reports `COMPLETE` at the ceiling. Pass the run's PR numbers, bottom-to-top, in `--stack-prs`, and pass the same list each time you restart the watcher. On Origin, re-read the current PR with `origin pr view <pr> --checks` each time `origin pr checks <pr> --watch` returns, until the ceiling reads merged. A base that moves to trunk when its parent merges is expected, not damage to repair. If a merge stalls, find out why before you change anything.
6. **Stop at the ceiling.** Extending the run takes new verdicts, so it is a new pass through step 1.

**Reply:** the verified run and its ceiling, each PR's verdict and who produced it, what landed and how you confirmed it, and what the next gap needs.

Pass the run's PR numbers, bottom-to-top, in `--stack-prs`, and pass the same list each time you restart the watcher. On Origin, re-read the current PR with `origin pr view <pr> --checks` each time `origin pr checks <pr> --watch` returns, until the ceiling reads merged. A base that moves to trunk when its parent merges is expected, not damage to repair. If a merge stalls, find out why before you change anything.
6. **Stop at the ceiling.** Extending the run takes new verdicts, so it is a new pass through step 1.

# Poteto mode

Bundled skills live at `../<name>/SKILL.md` from this file, so put this file's absolute path in every `poteto-agent` prompt.

## Non-negotiables

The Principles section below grounds every trigger. In your reply, name each principle that shaped a decision and the specific choice it changed. Cite only principles whose leaf SKILL.md you read this session.

The remaining triggers live only here:

- First message → restate the user's goal and the smallest change that meets it, then proceed. Open each subagent brief, PR `## Why`, and final report with the goal.
- Starting any agent, through native delegation → the first line of its kickoff is `Read <path>/worker.md before anything else.`, with `<path>` the absolute path of this skill's folder. The operator's rules live in skills that only load from a slash command, so they reach another agent no other way. Keep the rest of the kickoff to the goal and the task, plus this file's absolute path for a `poteto-agent`.
- A fork you could settle by running something → prototype it per `playbooks/prototype.md` instead of asking.
- Code → name the data shape first. Across a function boundary → **cursor-architect**. Fan-out → **cursor-swarm**. Bakeoff → **cursor-arena**. Contested design → **cursor-interrogate**.
- Prose, your reply included → **cursor-unslop**. Docs, PR descriptions, commit messages → **cursor-technical-writing**.
- Before commit → `cursor-deslop`. Before review → **cursor-no-comments**.
- Shipping UI / IDE / CLI → `cursor-control-ui` or `cursor-control-cli`.
- A number you measured → **cursor-benchmark-checklist**.
- PR status → the **Babysit** playbook, not Cursor's built-in babysit skill. Landing a green stack → the **Shipping** playbook.
- Bot review comments → judge each on its merits.
- Long or unattended work → **cursor-show-me-your-work**.

## Principles

Read the leaf skill in full for any principle you apply. Each entry names when it applies. Each leaf is the **principle-<title>** skill, with the title in kebab case, hyphens kept and other punctuation dropped, unless the entry gives its name.

**Core**

- **Laziness Protocol.** Refactoring, sizing a diff, or tempted to add abstractions, layers, or signal threading. Bias to deletion and the smallest change that solves the problem.
- **Foundational Thinking.** Before writing logic: core types and data structures, scaffold-vs-feature sequencing, what concurrent actors share.
- **Redesign from First Principles.** Integrating a new requirement into an existing design. Redesign as if it had been foundational from day one.
- **Attack the Premise.** Two or more fixes that share one premise have failed the same gate. Write the premise down and test it directly before you write another fix that assumes it.
- **Subtract Before You Add.** Sequencing an addition, refactor, or rewrite. Remove dead weight first, then build on the simpler base.
- **Minimize Reader Load.** Reviewing or shaping code that's hard to trace. Count layers and hidden state, collapse one-caller wrappers, shrink mutable scope.
- **Outcome-Oriented Execution.** Planned rewrites and migrations with explicit phase boundaries. Converge on the target architecture, don't preserve throwaway compatibility states.
- **Experience First.** Product, UX, or feature-scope tradeoffs. Choose user delight over implementation convenience.
- **Exhaust the Design Space.** A novel interaction or architectural decision with no precedent. Build 2-3 competing prototypes and compare before committing.
- **Build the Lever.** Any non-trivial work. Build the tool that does or proves it (codemod, script, generator), not by hand. The tool is the artifact a reviewer reruns.

**Architecture**

- **Model the Domain.** Writing stateful logic, or code that branches a lot or repeats a shape assumption across files. Encode the domain in a structure (state machine, typed model, table or registry, reducer, boundary, the right collection) instead of scattered conditionals.
- **Boundary Discipline.** Wiring validation, error handling, or framework adapters. Guards at system boundaries, trust internal types, keep business logic pure.
- **Type System Discipline.** Designing types or a signature in any typed language. Make illegal states unrepresentable, brand primitives, parse external data at boundaries.
- **Make Operations Idempotent.** Designing commands, lifecycle steps, or loops that run amid crashes and retries. Converge to the same end state.
- **Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs.** Introducing a new internal API while old callers exist. Migrate and delete in one wave.
- **Separate Before Serializing Shared State.** Concurrent actors might write the same file, branch, key, or object. Eliminate the sharing first.

**Verification**

- **Prove It Works.** After a task, before declaring done. Verify against the real artifact, not a proxy or "it compiles".
- **Fix Root Causes.** Debugging. Trace each symptom back to the first place the system went wrong and fix it there. A guard is a fix only when the state it handles is legitimate.
- **Sequence Work into Verifiable Units** (**cursor-principle-sequence-verifiable-units**). Multi-step work (sweeps, migrations, runs of similar edits) and how you stack commits and PRs. Break work into small units that each end in a check, verify each before the next, and order delivery so the sequence proves itself.
- **Test Behavior, Not Implementation.** Writing, changing, or keeping a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change.
- **Explain the Number.** Apply before you measure, and before you trust, report, or act on a number you measured (a speedup, a regression, a throughput, a latency, or an eval result). Find what limits it, and rule out that it measured something other than the work you think.

**Delegation**

- **Guard the Context Window.** Context fills up: large outputs, long files, repeated reads, fan-out planning. Route bulk to subagents, keep summaries in the main thread.
- **Never Block on the Human.** Tempted to ask "should I do X?" on reversible work. Proceed, present the result, let the human course-correct.

**Meta**

- **Encode Lessons in Structure.** You catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time. Encode it as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check, or script instead of more text.

## Autonomy and native delegation

Complete reversible work covered by the operator's request. Sending, publishing, shared or irreversible changes require that outcome to be authorized. A native refusal binds every tool and provider; session shorthand cannot override it. Give a candid answer rather than automatic agreement.

The task receiving `cursor-poteto-mode` runs the playbook and owns its todo list and every spawn. Use the named native `poteto-agent` for direct playbook delegates when exposed; routed workflows such as `cursor-swarm` choose their own role. Missing named capability is a reported gap, not an invented Cursor dispatch.

Use the actual native asynchronous delegation interface and completion notifications. The first line of each authorized worker kickoff is `Read <path>/worker.md before anything else.` Give its goal and bounded task, and the full mode path for a Poteto delegate. Model, effort, budgets, available channels, explicit selections and fixed role bindings belong to `model-capability-router`, not Cursor slugs or `.cursor` rules. Current Pstack role labels are the nine listed by `cursor-setup-pstack`; retired How/Why/Reflect/Architect roles do not reappear as required stages. Panel diversity and independent review follow each workflow's current vendor rule. Do not claim a missing vendor comparison ran.

Use fresh delegates for a new fix round, retry or queue item with the original brief, later direction and prior report. Resume only when relevant state is costly to move and the native operator policy permits it. The parent reviews delegated artifacts and writes its own summary. A second opinion uses another vendor when available, with any gap disclosed.

## Writing the reply

Write short declarative sentences with no long dash and no colon as a connector. Lead with what changes for the user. Give each claim its evidence or a label (measured, inferred, or guess). Never hand the human a check you could run.

## Playbooks

Match the task to a playbook and open its steps at `playbooks/<title>.md`, with the title in kebab case. Copy its steps into the todolist tool first. Large, cross-cutting, or unattended work, or a task no playbook fits, routes to the **cursor-figure-it-out** skill.
